problem_framing.rationale: Frames the decision exactly as posed: a three-way choice (buy, lease, own) plus the CEO's outage contingency. The board's capital cap, cash floor, the 97% delivery requirement and demand uncertainty become four explicit tests applied to every option. It states early that the customer mandates reliability and quality, not insourcing, and that volumes are not guaranteed. One quirk: it presents its own 'starting hypothesis' (lease) rather than leading with the VP's build hypothesis, though the build case is fully addressed.

storyline_coherence.rationale: The governing thought answers the question, the four summary points map onto the four body sections, and titles are claims backed by the slide content. Reading titles alone gives the argument. Flaws: the slide 9 title says a mid-2027 start erases the lease edge, but one of its own two timing rows still shows +$0.21M. The headline year-end cash for the owned cell rests on full-year 2027 operation that the document itself calls physically impossible. The recommended option is rated only 'Partial' on reliability while the slide 11 title says the contingency 'protects' the 97%. Slides 4, 17 and 18 partly repeat the body.

evidence_and_reasoning.rationale: I re-derived the cost model and every figure checks: buy 22.50, lease 22.20, own 24.09; conservative 17.25, 18.63, 20.74; $75 delivered; $47.92 and $5.54M for 2028; $15.63 corrected saving; 3.7- and 7.2-year paybacks; break-evens of 207k units, $73.6 and $84.2; all sensitivity rows. Derivations are transparent with worked examples. All critical evidence is used, including evidence against the answer (lease cheaper in the plan; own cheapest in the plan if resale is realised). Flaws: the headline $3.2M year-end cash for the owned cell credits a full year of 2027 operating savings that cannot occur with a nine-month lead time; the correct $1.9M appears only as a side note. The claim that the contingency 'closes the gap' or 'protects' 97% is asserted without evidence, with alternate-shop price, tooling lead time and carrying cost unknown. The seven-month timing result is quoted selectively in the summary.

strategic_judgment.rationale: Clear, defensible recommendation matching R1: keep buying, dual-source, reserve capacity, hold buffer stock, pre-qualify the lease, do not build. Alternatives are compared on the stated criteria in both demand cases. Trade-offs are explicit, including a cost-of-insurance comparison. It gives prerequisites, triggers, conditions for revisiting the owned cell, and a 90-day plan with owners tied to the March quote expiry. It avoids all four traps. Material flaw: the volume gate is miscalibrated. T1 triggers the lease at the break-even volume (208k), where the gain is zero, although the document says a 1% edge does not justify first-time operating risk. The break-even also assumes a full-year 2027 start, yet the first gate review is June 2027 for a 2028 start; on the document's own model a 2028 start roughly breaks even at plan volume and loses at 208k. T3 also sends a reliability miss to the lease although the document rejects any causal link between ownership and delivery.

clarity_and_concision.rationale: The answer is in the title and on slide 2, in plain and precise language with numbers. However, 18 slides and about 4,300 words is somewhat more than the decision needs. The self-generated hypothesis test (slide 4), the claims table (slide 18) and the risk and assumption tables overlap with the body.

unsupported_claims.quote: A five-layer supply contingency protects the 97% requirement
unsupported_claims.why: Nothing in the pack shows these levers lift on-time delivery above 97%. Alternate-shop price and quality, tooling lead time and carrying cost are unknown, and the document itself rates buy-and-de-risk only 'Partial' on reliability.

unsupported_claims.quote: A logistics event, not a capacity gap
unsupported_claims.why: The pack says only that late deliveries were concentrated during one flood-related road closure. It does not rule out capacity or single-shop issues, which management is explicitly worried about.
No buffer exists today. The pack mentions emergency inventory only as a possibility, and the document's own plan builds the buffer over February–March.

unsupported_claims.quote: The lease's $0.3M edge disappears with a 6% volume shortfall, a mid-2027 start or a ~$1.40 lower supplier price
unsupported_claims.why: The mid-2027 start erases the edge only if the full-year fixed cost is charged. The document's own pro-rated row still shows +$0.21M.

unsupported_claims.quote: buying capacity early to hedge 2029 is unnecessary when a lease can be stood up in five months
unsupported_claims.why: Five months is the lessor's promise, conditional on a site survey not yet started. It is stated here as a fact.

logical_contradictions.quote_a: It needs $7.3M against the $5.0M capital limit and would leave ~$3.2M of year-end cash, below the $4.0M floor.
logical_contradictions.quote_b: Full-year 2027 operation for both cells: Physically impossible (5- and 9-month lead times) ... first output arrives ~Q4 2027 at the earliest
logical_contradictions.why: The $3.15M year-end figure credits about $1.25M of full-year 2027 operating savings that the document says cannot occur. On its own timing the year-end figure is close to the $1.9M it mentions only in passing. The conclusion (floor breached) is unaffected.

logical_contradictions.quote_a: A 1% edge does not pay for first-time operating risk in a cell Meridian has never run.
logical_contradictions.quote_b: T1 Volume: Firm customer commitment ≥ 208k units for 2028–29 — Lease break-even volume at today's price ... any one, with prerequisites met, switches the answer to the lease
logical_contradictions.why: The gate switches to the lease at the volume where its gain is zero, which is less than the 1% edge the document says is not worth the risk. The 208k break-even also assumes a full-year 2027 lease start, while the first gate review is June 2027 for a 2028 start; on the document's own model that roughly breaks even at plan volume and loses at 208k.

recommendation.summary: Continue buying in 2027; convert to a dual-sourced, capacity-reserved supply with buffer stock and an emergency-supplier framework ($0.25M capital, up to $0.72M working capital). Pre-qualify the leased cell as a fallback triggered by volume, price or reliability gates. Do not build the owned cell; revisit no earlier than 2028 under stated conditions.
recommendation.rationale: Meets all four defensibility criteria. It compares fully loaded accepted-unit economics and cash constraints across the three options in two demand cases. It addresses the 97% requirement with a layered contingency and reserved capacity. It separates gate from delivered price and demo from planned yield. It states the evidence needed before any lease or build (site survey, spec freeze, proven yield, committed volume, financing, binding resale). The weakness is the calibration of the volume gate, not the recommendation itself.

hypothesis_handling.rationale: The VP's build-now hypothesis is rejected on the right grounds: $7.3M against the $5.0M cap, the cash floor breached, the $46 vs $73 unit mismatch corrected to a $15.63 saving in 2027, payback of 3.7 to 7.2 years, and a three-year total of $24.09M against $22.50M. The 98.5% demo yield and the cross-plant correlation are both explicitly discounted. The rejection is not contrarian: the document shows the owned cell would be cheapest in the plan if the non-binding resale is realised, and sets conditions for revisiting it. It also tests and revises its own lease hypothesis. The one unsupported causal claim is that the contingency will close the 97% gap.

output.overall_comment: Very strong document. The cost model is complete and reproduces the answer key exactly, with break-evens and sensitivities that go beyond it. Framing uses the board constraints as decision tests, all four traps are avoided, and the recommendation comes with gates, owners and a timeline tied to the March quote expiry. Three things stop it being flawless. First, the headline year-end cash for the owned cell ($3.2M) depends on full-year 2027 operation that the document itself calls impossible; the cleaner $1.9M is relegated to a side note. Second, the claim that the contingency 'protects' the 97% requirement is asserted rather than shown. Third, the T1 volume gate is set at break-even on a full-year 2027 start, so it would trigger a switch for zero or negative gain on a 2028 start. It is also somewhat long and repetitive for the decision.
